Excellencies, colleagues, representatives from the OPD movement, friends, welcome to the COSP side event, Financing Disability Inclusion at Scale, focused on mobilizing domestic resources as well as international financing in the next decade of the CRPD. Many Governments have updated their laws, legislations, enacted new ones. We have seen strengthening of national coordination mechanisms, programmes on disability inclusion. We have seen more visibility on disability inclusion across health, education, social protection, assistive technology and across sectors. The key question now is that is financing keeping pace. Of course, we have seen that many governments have expanded domestic financing. International cooperation around this area has grown, but it is not yet enough to meet the political commitments, the legal obligations, and to ensure the CRPD actually can be implemented to change the realities of the lives of persons with disabilities on the ground. The starting level has been low, but opportunities exist. And today, this event will explore how governments, UN agencies, organizations of persons with disabilities, other financing partners can come together and expand as well as align better the financing of disability inclusion at scale, including through the Amman-Berlin Declaration. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities has transformed our understanding of disability from a welfare and charity perspective to a human right-based approach that recognizes persons with disabilities as equal right holders and active contributors to societies. As we approach the 20th anniversary of the Convention, we are reminded that our effort must focus not only on protecting rights, but also on expanding opportunities for meaningful participation, economic empowerment, and social inclusion. We are also strengthening disability data and evidence-based policy making to better identify barriers and support inclusive developments. We express our sincere gratitude for UNICEF's continued partnership and steadfast support in promoting the rights, inclusion and dignity of persons with disability in Timor-Leste. This dialogue provides a valuable platform for Timor-Leste to share its national efforts to strengthening disability inclusive budgeting undertaken in alignment with our obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, CRPD, and guided by the National Disability Action Plan 2021-2030. Since the ratification of the CRPD in 2023, Timor-Leste has pursued a series of concrete and strategic measures to enhance the visibility, coherence and accountability of disability-related investments across government. First, the government of Timor-Leste has introduced in 2026 a disability inclusion budget marker that enables the systematic identification and classification of disability-related expenditures within the national budget Therefore, a strengthening transparency, accountability, evidence-based decision-making, while supporting more coordinated planning, budgeting, and monitoring across all sectors. Second, Timor-Leste has a strengthening cross-sectoral collaboration among the 11 line ministries, led by the Minister of Social Solidarity and Inclusion and the Minister of Finance, together with development partners and organizations of persons with disabilities. This enhanced cooperation has helped institutionalize the understanding that disability inclusion is a cross-cutting responsibility, requiring coherent and coordinated action across education, health, social protection, employment, accessibility and community development. Disability considerations have been integrated into national planning and budgeting guidelines. Tools and guidance have been developed to support line ministries in applying the disability inclusion budget marker and in reporting on disability-related expenditures. Fourth, the government has undertaken capacity-building initiatives for officials at national and municipal levels to strengthen their ability to integrate disability perspectives into planning, budgeting, and monitoring. These efforts are essential to embedding disability inclusion with public financial management systems. Excellencies, Timor-Leste underscored the importance of strengthening international cooperation and technical partnership to advance disability inclusion budgeting and to further refine the national disability marker for disability budget tracking. In line with its obligation under the CRPD, Timor-Leste recalls that Article 4.2 calls upon State parties to mobilize the maximum available resources and, where necessary, to seek international cooperation to progressively realize the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 31 requires the collection of appropriate data. Every 10 years, Timor-Leste holds a national census to inform evidence-based policy making, and Article 33 mandates effective national implementation and monitoring framework, while the CRPD does not explicitly reference a disability marker, this provision collectively provide the normative basis for development tools that enhance visibility, accountability and tracking a disability related investment. DMO Leste therefore welcomes continued collaboration with development partners, UN agency and organizations of persons with disability to strengthen the national capacity, improve data systems and ensure the public finance effectively advances the rights and inclusion of all persons with disabilities. Despite these important advances, it recognizes that significant challenges remain. Disability budget tracking is still at early stage of development. Further efforts are required to strengthen data systems and has institutional coordination and establish clear and more consistent methodology for identify and monitoring disability related expenditure. Improving disability disaggregated disaggregated data also remains a priority to support more robust evidence-based policy making. Looking ahead, Timor-Leste has identified several priority areas: strengthening disability responsive budgeting across all sectors, developing more robust and user-friendly tracking tools, improving disability disaggregated data, ensuring meaningful participation of persons with disability and their representative organizations, institutional capacity at national and municipal levels, expanding technical cooperation and knowledge exchange with international partners. Timor-Leste firmly believes that effective budget tracking is essential to ensuring accountability and translating commitments into tangible improvements in the lives of persons with disability. In closing, Timor-Leste reaffirms its strong commitment to working closely with UNICEF, development and organizations of persons with disabilities to advance inclusive public financing and to ensure the full participation of persons with disabilities at national development. I would like to share with you some of the insights that you can find online in the background paper on financing acceleration of disability inclusion that we did for the Global Disability Inclusion Report for GDS 2025. We did the most comprehensive to date comparative analysis of national budget in low and middle income countries with regards to disability specific expenditure. Getting data is not easy, and I really want to congratulate Timor-Leste, because the more country will use trackers and marker, the easier it will be to do this kind of work. So what we've seen is the emergence of two benchmark. We have a first group of countries that are what we consider initial level of investment. which is usually between 0.01% of GDP and 0.1% of GDP. And often countries that have different type of programs, but maybe that are either a bit fragmented or not reaching sufficient scale. Then we have another group of countries that are at 0.1% of GDP, and there is a kind of clarity there. It's countries that start to have program, notably social protection and cash transfer, that get to scale. And finally, we have a smaller group of countries that are around 0.5% of GDP, which is basically countries that have programs at scale with relative adequacy. If we translate that to share of national budget, it ranges from 0.07 to 2.1% of national budget. As an order of comparison, OECD countries spend in average solely on social protection for disability, 1.5% of GDP. What we looked also is what was the distribution of expenditure between sectors, and unsurprisingly to many of you, we see a concentration of expenditure in three ministries or sectors: health, education, and social protection. And what is really striking is that the biggest driver to increase disability-related expenditure is social protection. It's basically the program that goes to scale the fastest and drive breaking the ceiling of 0.1% of GDP. One thing or so that we did, and you will be able to see that in the report in more detail, is that over most of the countries we've looked at, there has been increase of expenditure for person with disabilities in recent years in real values as a share of GDP, as well as a share of government expenditure, ranging from 28% expenditure all the way to 300% increase of expenditure. And even in some countries where significant economic crises have happened, for instance, Argentina in past years, we've seen that there might have been a decrease in real value of the budget for person with disabilities, but it was fairly resilient and retain a certain increase in share of GDP. So next, we tried to estimate the financing gap. And we had a lot of-- we discussed with many partners. We had a lot of ambition. And it has been much more difficult than we thought because there is not enough evidence. We had a lot of difficulties to find costed intervention at scale. What does it mean to do inclusive education at scale? How much does it cost to bring assistive technology at scale, to bring community supports, et cetera? So we see, and this is a very nice and important trend, an increasing number of countries that have costed disability strategy or national disability action plan, which is helpful. For instance, Zimbabwe, Mauritania, Rwanda, and some other countries here. And what we try to do is focusing on, for instance, disability cash benefit or extension of health insurance, because technically they are easier to do. And We did that over five countries and we saw that whatever the scenario we took, whether it was a normative scenario or a more realistic national scenario, expenditure were at least three times more than what is currently being spent, up to 10 times. We looked also at different channel of financing, how money flows from domestic revenue, grants or borrowing. I won't go into all the details, you will see that in the report. But one thing we did, and you can also find it online, we did the first review of national disability funds in low and middle income countries. Why? Because many disability rights legislation install a national fund for persons with disabilities. And actually, there is no real evidence on how those funds work, what are their added value. So I invite you to look at the paper we did on this. What we see is that one of the issue is that many of those funds do not have clear objective. What are they supposed to do in addition to what ministries have been doing? So for instance, Some do, like in Kenya, there are two funds that have fairly specific objectives, but in some circumstances, it's not so easy to understand what is the added value of the fund. Another issue is also the lack of specific revenue for the funds. Few countries have, for instance, quota levy with regards to employment, but often the money that goes in the fund comes from the general budget. So the question is, The money that goes in the fund, is it money that is going in the fund instead of going to line ministries working on inclusion, or it's on top of the money that is going to line ministries and local government? What we've seen in the recent years is that There has been an increase in reporting of disability inclusive ODA thanks to the OECD DAC marker. The first thing, and we will hear more today about it, the ensuring meaningful OPD participation and budgeting processes. We found some evidence. I always give the example of sign language interpreter systems. No ministry can finance it alone, but it falls between the cracks. And at the end, because there is no common financing mechanism for such services that education, health, justice, and others need, those systems do not develop. We need stronger evidence and tracking, and we need Costing priority reform at scale and defining realistic financing pathways, embedding disability inclusion and those costed scenarios in national development plan and financing strategy. Also making better use of existing expenditure, public procurement is a fantastic tool. where accessibility requirement could leverage much more inclusive expenditure. And we didn't find clear evidence that many countries were actually using those mechanisms to really leverage.
